tasks.q: What is the purpose of the CPU?
a: To process data and instructions by fetching, decoding and executing them
To display images on the screen
To connect the computer to the internet
tasks.fb: Storage, display and networking are done by other components.
It's the central part that processes everything.

tasks.q: During the fetch stage, what happens to the program counter?
a: It is incremented to point to the next instruction
It stores the result of a calculation
tasks.fb: The PC always holds the address of the next instruction, so it moves on by one.

tasks.q: Where is the instruction fetched from?
tasks.fb: Programs being run are held in RAM.
The CU works out what each instruction means.

tasks.q: What does 'decode' mean in the fetch-decode-execute cycle?
a: Working out what the instruction means and what needs to be done
Sending the instruction to the printer
tasks.fb: Only once it's decoded can the instruction be carried out.

tasks.q: Where are the results of calculations stored?
tasks.fb: The ALU does the maths and the accumulator holds the answer.

tasks.q: After the execute stage, what happens next?
a: The cycle starts again with the next fetch
The CPU waits for the user to press a key
tasks.fb: The cycle repeats billions of times a second.

tasks.q: Match each register to its purpose.
pairs: Holds the address of the next instruction
Holds the address where data is to be stored or fetched
Holds data fetched from, or to be written to, main memory
tasks.fb: This is Task 2 on your worksheet and a very common exam question.

tasks.q: Match each component to what it does.
pairs: Decodes instructions and controls how data moves around the CPU
Fast memory for frequently used instructions and data
tasks.fb: Use the 3D CPU model to see where the cache sits.

tasks.q: Why is cache faster to use than RAM?
a: It is inside the CPU, very close to where the processing happens
tasks.fb: Cache is the worktop next to the chef: fewer things fit, but they're within reach.

tasks.q: Put the steps of the fetch-decode-execute cycle in order.
steps: The PC holds the address of the next instruction
The address is copied into the MAR
The instruction is fetched from RAM into the MDR
The PC is incremented to point to the next instruction
The control unit decodes the instruction
tasks.fb: Then the whole cycle repeats for the next instruction.

info.title: The first microprocessor
info.text: The Intel 4004, released in 1971, was the first CPU on a single chip. It had about 2,300 transistors; modern CPUs have billions.

info.title: Billions per second
info.text: A 3 GHz CPU can run about 3 billion cycles every second, so the fetch-decode-execute cycle happens faster than you can imagine.

info.title: Instruction sets
info.text: Each type of CPU understands its own set of instructions. PCs mostly use x86 CPUs, while phones and many new laptops use ARM.

info.title: Hot stuff
info.text: CPUs get hot while they work. Many slow themselves down automatically if they reach around 100°C, to avoid damage.

info.title: Registers are tiny
info.text: A register holds just one value, but it's the fastest memory in the whole computer.

info.title: The kitchen analogy
info.text: Cache is like the worktop next to you: only a few things fit, but they're within reach. RAM is the cupboard across the kitchen, and storage is the shop down the road.

models.title: Inside a CPU
models.text: Turn the CPU and click its parts. The metal lid is see-through, so you can see the cores and cache inside.

models.title: The motherboard
models.text: See where the CPU sits, how it's kept cool, and where RAM goes.
